messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Niran had spent years moving through his work as a dancer with the discipline of someone who knew how to keep time in his body, but the war zone deployment had broken that certainty in a single evening. He had gone there as a relief worker, moving between damaged buildings and crowded shelters, and on one assignment he was caught in a scene that he now described with a mixture of dread and disgust: the air thick with smoke, the sting of alcohol from spilled antiseptic or liquor in the chaos, and the bitter smell of something burnt hanging over the street as he tried to help people who were screaming and half-blinded by dust. It was the same time of day now that could still catch him off guard, the hour when the light began to fade and the air changed, and he had come to dread that shift in the day because it made the memory feel dangerously close. When that hour arrived, or when he passed a bar and caught alcohol on someone’s breath, or when a burnt smell drifted from a kitchen or a trash can outside his building, something in his surroundings could instantly pull him back into the full scene without warning. He would feel his chest lock, his attention narrow, and the event would not come back as a story he was telling himself; it would arrive as if it were happening again, right now, with the same helpless urgency and the same sense that he was still standing in that street.

The way the memory returned did not stay neutral for long. Niran felt intense shame whenever it hit him, because what came up with the image of that evening was not only fear but the thought that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. He kept replaying the moments when he believed he should have done more, should have been steadier, faster, kinder, or somehow less overwhelmed. As he described it in therapy, the memory and the shame fed each other: the more vividly the scene came back, the more he judged himself for how he had behaved there, and the more he judged himself, the more unbearable and immediate the memory became. He was certain that the way he had reacted since the event proved he was a lousy coper, and that belief sat close to the surface whenever the recollection took hold. He could not trust himself, he said, because if he had failed once in that place, he might fail again in front of his family, his students, or anyone who needed him.

Those beliefs also changed how he moved through daily life. Niran began scanning his surroundings with particular vigilance, bracing for the same time of day and for the smells that seemed to summon the episode before he had time to prepare. He noticed the burnt odor from a neighbor’s cooking in the hallway of the apartment building they shared, and he would tense before he even knew why. At his dance studio, where he taught classes in the late afternoon, he found himself preoccupied with who might come in smelling of alcohol after work, and with whether the room would carry the scent of a burned bulb or a heater. Because he could not rely on himself, he started avoiding some errands near dusk and limiting his time in places where those cues were more likely to appear. He told himself that this vigilance was necessary, because if he let his guard down he would be taken back by surprise and collapse into the same shameful, helpless state. Yet the more he watched for danger, the more often he seemed to find it, and the more often he found it, the more his confidence in himself eroded.

Over the months this pattern narrowed his life in quiet but concrete ways. He became less present at home, more irritable with his wife, and increasingly preoccupied during rehearsals, as though part of him were always waiting for the next scent or hour to turn against him. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he was beginning to miss classes and social obligations because he could not trust himself to remain steady when the evening came or when a smell struck him unexpectedly. He came in frightened that he was becoming smaller around his own life, and what he most hoped for was some way to stand in those moments without being dragged straight back into the war zone, ashamed of himself before the memory had even finished arriving.
